description: Christian belief in revelation through the Bible and Jesus, visions, miracles and Humanist counter-arguments.
content_html:
Revelation: How God Makes Himself Known

Revelation is the means by which God communicates himself and his purposes to human beings. Christians believe that God has revealed himself progressively throughout history. A key framework for understanding this is the idea of covenants — formal agreements God established with key figures that progressively disclosed his character and plan. The covenant with Noah (Genesis 6–9) promised that God would never again destroy all life by flood, revealing his faithfulness and mercy. The covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15, 17) promised him descendants as numerous as the stars and a land for his people, revealing God as a personal God who initiates relationships.

The New Testament presents Jesus as the culmination of all revelation. Hebrews 1:1–4 states: “In the past God spoke to our ancestors through the prophets at many times and in various ways, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son.” For Christians across denominations, Jesus is not just a messenger but the living Word of God — the fullest possible expression of who God is and what he is like.

Key Fact

The covenant with Noah reveals God’s faithfulness and care for all creation. The covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15) reveals God as a personal God who initiates a relationship with a chosen people. Both are examples of God’s gradual self-disclosure that culminates in Jesus (Hebrews 1:1–4).

Visions as Evidence for God

Throughout the Bible, God communicates through visions. Genesis 15 records God appearing to Abraham in a vision, showing him the stars and promising him descendants — this covenant vision is foundational to the entire biblical story. Matthew 17:1–13 records the Transfiguration: Jesus takes Peter, James and John up a mountain where his appearance is transformed — his face shines like the sun and his clothes become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear with him, and God’s voice declares from a cloud: “This is my Son, whom I love; with him I am well pleased. Listen to him.”

Christians understand the Transfiguration as a vision that revealed Jesus’s divine nature to his disciples. It confirmed their belief that he was not merely a prophet (like Moses or Elijah) but the Son of God himself. Christians today may have their own experiences of visions — reported encounters with God, angels or deceased saints — though different denominations respond to these with varying degrees of openness: Catholics have a formal process of approval for reported visions; many Protestants emphasise that scripture is the primary source of revelation.

Catholic Christianity has a tradition of formally recognised visions — Lourdes, Fatima, and the visions of Joan of Arc are evaluated by Church authority and may be approved. Catholics believe the Church’s Magisterium can discern genuine visions from false ones. Most Protestant and evangelical Christians emphasise that the Bible alone (sola scriptura) contains the authoritative revelation, and personal visions should always be tested against scripture. Some Pentecostal and charismatic Christians actively expect ongoing prophetic visions and experiences, believing the Spirit continues to reveal God directly to believers today. What unites all these views is agreement that God is capable of communicating with human beings — the debate is about the channels and the authority they carry.

Miracles as Evidence for God

A miracle is an event that goes beyond what science can explain, which believers attribute to God. Christians point to the miracles of Jesus as evidence both that God exists and that Jesus is who he claimed to be. John 4:43–54 records one such sign: a royal official whose son was near death asked Jesus for help. Jesus told him to go home, that his son would live. The official trusted Jesus’s word, and when he returned home, his servants told him his son had recovered at the exact moment Jesus had spoken. This sign strengthened the faith of the official’s whole household.

Atheists and Humanists challenge the evidential value of both visions and miracles. Scottish philosopher David Hume (1711–1776) argued that the uniform experience of natural law makes it always more rational to doubt a miracle report than to accept it — it is always more likely that the witnesses were mistaken, deceived or self-deceived than that an actual law of nature was suspended. Modern atheists such as Richard Dawkins argue that religious visions are hallucinations produced by brain chemistry, not genuine encounters with God. Humanists add that belief in miracles encourages people to reject medicine and science in favour of prayer and superstition. Christians respond that these objections assume the answer before looking at the evidence, and that the documented cases of miraculous healing and the transformed lives of vision-recipients cannot simply be dismissed.

Key Fact

David Hume argued in the eighteenth century that natural law is so reliable that it is always more rational to doubt a miracle report than to accept it. Christians respond that this assumes the conclusion before examining evidence, and that Hume’s argument would equally dismiss well-attested historical events that are surprising but real.
exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark “Explain Two with Sources,” cite either Hebrews 1:1–4 (revelation through Jesus) or Genesis 15 (Abraham covenant vision) or John 4:43–54 (the royal official’s son). A paraphrase without the reference earns only 4 marks at most. For the 12-mark Discuss question, remember to develop the Hume/Dawkins counter-argument in full — examiners note that students often write only one sentence on the opposing view. For divergent Christian views on visions, contrast Catholic (formal approval process, Magisterium) with Protestant (scripture as the primary test). SPaG marks reward correct spelling of: covenant, revelation, Transfiguration, Hume.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians believe God has revealed himself through covenants (Noah, Abraham) and most fully through Jesus — Hebrews 1:1–4 establishes Jesus as God’s definitive Word.
  • The Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1–13) and the covenant vision to Abraham (Genesis 15) are key biblical visions used as evidence for God’s existence and character. Different denominations differ on how to evaluate claimed visions today.
  • Miracles, such as the healing of the royal official’s son (John 4:43–54), are used as evidence of divine action; Hume and Dawkins challenge this, but Christians argue these objections beg the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline three Christian beliefs about revelation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for each of three discrete points: God has revealed himself through the prophets and scriptures (1); the covenants with Noah and Abraham are key moments of revelation showing God's faithfulness and personal concern (1); Jesus Christ is the fullest and final revelation of God — Hebrews 1:1-4 (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe what Christians believe happened at the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:1-13).
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: Jesus took Peter, James and John up a mountain (1); his face shone like the sun and his clothes became white as light; Moses and Elijah appeared with him (1); God's voice declared from a cloud 'This is my Son whom I love — listen to him' (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe the covenants with Noah and Abraham provide evidence for God's existence.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason (1 for a stated point, 2 for a developed explanation). For example: The covenant with Noah shows God's care and faithfulness to all creation — God promises never to destroy all life by flood again, revealing a personal God who acts in history (2); the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15) is a visionary encounter in which God promises descendants as numerous as the stars, showing God initiates personal relationships and makes binding promises (2).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Christians believe miracles provide evidence for the existence of God, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per reason; 1 mark for a named source. Example: The healing in John 4:43-54 — where the official's son recovered at the exact moment Jesus spoke — suggests God has power over natural processes, supporting belief in an omnipotent creator (2); miracles produce faith in those who witness them, suggesting they originate from a divine source rather than natural coincidence (2); source credit for citing John 4:43-54 or Hebrews 1:1-4 explicitly (1).

practice_questions.text:
'Miracles and visions prove that God exists.'
Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10-12): Both sides developed with named sources; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Christian case: miracles (John 4:43-54) and visions (Genesis 15, Matthew 17:1-13) show God communicating directly; transformed lives and unexplained healings support this. Counter: Hume's argument that natural law always makes doubt more rational than acceptance; Dawkins on visions as brain chemistry; only anecdote supports miracles. Evaluate which position is stronger with reasoning. Secure (7-9): Both sides present, source named. Developing (4-6): One side dominant. Emerging (1-3): Brief, one-sided. SPaG: revelation, covenant, Transfiguration.

practice_questions.text: Explain two divergent Christian views about visions, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per view; 1 mark for a named source. Example: Catholic Christianity formally evaluates reported visions through the Church's Magisterium — only approved visions are accepted as reliable, with Hebrews 1:1-4 confirming that any vision must align with Christ as the fullness of revelation (2); many Protestant Christians hold that scripture (sola scriptura) is the sole reliable source of revelation, so personal visions should always be tested against biblical teaching — the Transfiguration (Matthew 17) is paradigmatic but personal visions today are secondary to scripture (2); source credit for Hebrews 1:1-4 or Matthew 17:1-13 explicitly named (1).

knowledge_checks.q: What does Hebrews 1:1-4 teach about how God has spoken 'in these last days'?
options: Through the prophets of the Old Testament
Through visions given to the disciples

knowledge_checks.q: What was David Hume's argument against miracles?
options: Miracles are only recorded in the Old Testament and are therefore irrelevant today
Natural law is so reliable that it is always more rational to doubt a miracle report than to accept it
The disciples lied about seeing Jesus perform miracles
God would not need to perform miracles if he were all-powerful

knowledge_checks.q: In Matthew 17:1-13, the event in which Jesus's divine glory was revealed on the mountain is called the _____.
In Genesis 15, God appeared to Abraham in a vision and promised him descendants as numerous as the _____.
Match each scripture to its significance for revelation:
right: Jesus as God's fullest revelation in 'these last days'
God's covenant vision to Abraham promising descendants
Jesus heals the royal official's son — a miracle sign

flashcard_questions.q: What are the two main Old Testament covenants named in Christian revelation teaching for this course?
flashcard_questions.a: The covenant with Noah (never to destroy all life again) and the covenant with Abraham (descendants as stars).
God appearing to Abraham in a vision, promising him descendants as numerous as the stars.
Jesus's face shone like the sun, Moses and Elijah appeared, and God's voice declared Jesus as his beloved Son.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Hebrews 1:1-4 teach about Jesus and revelation?
flashcard_questions.a: God spoke through prophets in the past but speaks most fully through his Son in 'these last days'.

flashcard_questions.q: What miracle is recorded in John 4:43-54?
flashcard_questions.a: Jesus heals a royal official's son at a distance — the boy recovered at the exact moment Jesus spoke.

flashcard_questions.q: Who was David Hume and what was his argument about miracles?
flashcard_questions.a: A Scottish philosopher (1711-1776) who argued natural law makes it always more rational to doubt miracle reports than accept them.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between Catholic and Protestant responses to claimed visions today?
flashcard_questions.a: Catholics have a formal Magisterium approval process; Protestants test all claims against scripture (sola scriptura).

flashcard_questions.q: What is a 'covenant' in biblical terms?
flashcard_questions.a: A binding agreement between God and humanity through which God reveals his character and purposes.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Christian view of miracles as evidence for God?
flashcard_questions.a: Miracles show God's power over natural processes and his direct involvement in the world.

flashcard_questions.q: What is Richard Dawkins's main objection to religious visions?
flashcard_questions.a: Visions are hallucinations produced by brain chemistry, not genuine encounters with God.

glossary_terms.definition: God making himself known to humanity through the natural world, scripture, covenants, and most fully through Jesus Christ.
A binding agreement or promise between God and humanity — such as those with Noah and Abraham — through which God reveals his character and purposes.
The biblical patriarch with whom God established a covenant promising never again to destroy all life — evidence of God's faithfulness (Genesis 6-9).
The patriarch with whom God made a covenant in Genesis 15 and 17, promising descendants as numerous as the stars.
A supernatural experience in which a person believes they have seen or encountered God or a heavenly being, often accompanied by a divine message.
An event that appears to go beyond natural explanation and is attributed to the direct action of God.
A Scottish philosopher (1711-1776) who argued that natural law is so reliable that it is always more rational to doubt a miracle report than to accept it.
